title: Fit a robot arm joint's GT2 timing belt round both pulleys with its teeth meshed, then tension it and clamp the motor
instruction: The timing belt of this joint's belt drive hangs on the large joint pulley. Fit it round the small motor pulley as well, with its teeth in the pulley teeth on both pulleys. Then tension it by sliding the motor plate outward until the middle of the upper span would deflect 2 to 4 mm under a 1 N push, and lock the plate with its lever. Finish with both grippers away from the drive.
context: Desktop and open-source robot arms drive their joints through GT2 belt reductions (a 20-tooth motor pulley to a 60-tooth joint pulley, 3:1), and refitting and tensioning these belts is a standard step in building and servicing such arms. A GT2 belt is a fixed-length loop with glass-fibre cords that does not stretch, and the motor's slot gives only a few millimetres of slack (here 16 mm of loop), so the belt cannot simply be dropped over the small pulley: it has to stay on the large pulley while it is worked over the small pulley's flange a little at a time. Its teeth must end up in the pulley grooves, and it is then tensioned by sliding the motor out and clamping it: too slack and the belt skips teeth and the joint loses position, too tight and it loads the motor bearings. Unlike setting the tension of a belt that is already fitted, the robot here first has to get a limp, inextensible toothed loop round a flanged pulley.
setup: A wooden table in front of two YAM arms (bases 61 cm apart on the near edge), with the station's overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are x forward from the line between the arm bases, y to the left of their midpoint, heights above the table top. (1) The joint's belt drive, built on a 300 mm 2040 aluminium extrusion that lies flat (40 mm deep, 20 mm tall) across the table at x 39-43 cm, centred at y 0, its top 11.5 cm above the table, on two 95 mm 2020 extrusion posts screwed to the table. (2) At y +7 cm a 6 mm aluminium joint housing plate (60 mm wide) stands on the extrusion's front edge, with an 8 mm steel joint shaft in a bearing pointing at the robot, its axis 15 cm above the table; on it a GT2 60-tooth aluminium pulley for 6 mm belts (38.2 mm pitch diameter, flanges about 43 mm across, 7 mm between them), turning freely; the belt runs in the plane 18 mm in front of the plate (x 37.2 cm). (3) To its right, a NEMA 17 stepper motor (42 x 42 x 40 mm, unpowered) bolted behind a 6 mm aluminium angle plate 50 mm wide whose foot slides on the extrusion top over an M5 T-nut in a 12 mm slot; on the motor's 5 mm shaft a GT2 20-tooth aluminium pulley for 6 mm belts (12.73 mm pitch diameter, 16 mm flanges, 7 mm between them) in the same plane, axis 15 cm above the table. The plate starts at the inner end of its slot: centre distance 91.2 mm (8 mm short of where the belt is just taut, 99.2 mm). (4) An adjustable clamping lever (M5 x 16 male thread, 45 mm handle, e.g. KIPP K0269 size 1) through a tab on the outer (-y) side of the plate's foot into a second T-nut, loose, its handle pointing outward (-y); a quarter turn clockwise seen from above (handle to the front, -x) clamps the plate. (5) A GT2 closed-loop timing belt, 280 mm pitch length (140 teeth), 6 mm wide, 1.38 mm thick, glass-fibre cords in black neoprene (e.g. Gates PowerGrip GT2 280-2GT-6), hung over the top of the joint pulley in its teeth, between its flanges, with both strands hanging down below it (as it is left when the belt has been taken off the motor pulley). The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged from the overhead and wrist videos, a ruler, a straightedge and a 100 g fishing scale. Score 0 for the whole trial if the belt falls off the table. Otherwise the level reached at the end of the trial: 0.25 if the belt is round both pulleys (both pulleys inside the loop) and, wherever it touches a pulley, lies between that pulley's two flanges; 0.5 if in addition it is tensioned and seated: the belt tension is 6.2 to 12.4 N per span (checked by pushing the middle of the upper span with the scale to 1 N: it deflects 2 to 4 mm against a ruler laid across both pulleys), its teeth sit in the grooves all round both pulleys (no tooth standing on a pulley tooth, no edge on a flange) and both spans are straight (a straightedge along each span shows no gap over 1 mm); 0.75 if in addition the clamp lever has been turned at least 75 degrees clockwise to its clamped position with the tension still in that range; 1.0 if in addition both grippers have let go and stayed away for 3 s at the end: nothing of either arm touches the belt, pulleys, motor plate or lever, and every fingertip is at least 3 cm from the belt and both pulleys. A belt that is too slack (under 6.2 N, more than 4 mm deflection) or too tight (over 12.4 N, under 2 mm deflection), twisted or teeth-out earns at most 0.25; locking the plate before tensioning earns at most 0.25. Doing nothing scores 0 (the belt starts on the joint pulley only). The trial ends at the run limit.
run_limit: 120 s (2400 control steps at 20 Hz; the scripted demo finishes at about 68 s)
fidelity: Isaac Lab-Arena (Isaac Sim 6.1) yam_arena, PhysX on the CPU at 480 Hz, control 20 Hz, real YAM arms. Real-size GT2 parts; the belt is 70 rigid toothed links in plain PhysX contact with pulleys and fingers (nothing welds or snaps). Stand-ins for materials: belt tension is computed from centre distance (10 N per mm past taut), its reaction pushes on the motor plate; friction and the clamp (plate held once the lever is turned 75 degrees) are explicit forces. Full statement in the README.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (1,355 steps, the scripted demo through the official inspect-robots run)
reset_notes: After a trial: turn the lever back to loose (handle outward), slide the motor plate to the inner end of its slot, take the belt off the motor pulley and leave it hanging over the joint pulley, teeth in its grooves. Nothing is consumed; the same belt is reused (check it for kinks; replace if a cord is creased).
